title: Association between e-cigarette use, physical activity and cardiorespiratory fitness: protocol for a systematic review

sections.abstract:
Despite the rise in popularity of e-cigarette smoking or ‘vaping’, its long-term health consequences are still being investigated. In particular, it is unclear what impact e-cigarette use has on aerobic performance and exercise capacity. This information has important implications both for tobacco smokers as a harm reduction approach, and youth and young adults who are increasingly turning to e-cigarettes recreationally. Thus, this review aims to systematically evaluate the literature surrounding the effects of regular e-cigarette use on markers of cardiorespiratory fitness and physical activity.

This protocol follows the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols guidelines. A systematic search was undertaken in October 2024, using the defined population, intervention, comparison, outcomes, study time framework to identify all relevant articles. Studies will be eligible if they include individuals who use e-cigarette products, assess regular e-cigarette use as an exposure, compare to a group of non-users and report outcomes related to measures of cardiorespiratory fitness (eg, VO2max, 6 min walk test) or physical activity (eg, sport participation, meeting weekly physical activity guidelines), regardless of study duration. Searched databases will include PubMed/Medline, Cochrane Library and Embase, with no restriction to date or language of publication. Two reviewers will carry out the title and abstract screening, full text review and data extraction. Risk of bias will be assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for non-randomised studies and the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool (v2) for randomised studies. Study heterogeneity will be assessed using the Q and I 2 statistic tests. Efforts will be made to conduct a meta-analysis if sufficient data and homogeneity are present. Otherwise, a narrative synthesis will be conducted, focusing on common themes, subgroups and sources of variability.

Ethics approval is not required for this review of previously published or presented data. The results of the review will be disseminated via conference presentations and peer-reviewed publication. Moreover, results of this review may inform public health recommendations and identify areas in the field where further research is needed.

sections.introduction:
Data from 2022 spanning Canada, England and the USA suggest that 15%–24% of youth aged 16–19 have used electronic cigarettes (e-cigarettes) in the past 30 days. 1 Use of e-cigarettes or ‘vaping’, was originally marketed as a healthier alternative to tobacco smoking and an approach to smoking cessation. 2 However, there has also been an increase in ‘recreational’ e-cigarette use in those who are not tobacco smokers, especially among younger people. 1

The long-term detrimental aspects of cigarette smoking have been well characterised. 3 In contrast, e-cigarettes have only been around since the start of the 21st century, so their effect on clinical outcomes is still being investigated. 4 Studying the effects of e-cigarettes is further complicated by the fact that there is great variability in e-cigarette devices, nicotine content and e-liquid composition. 5 Nonetheless, there is some evidence to suggest that use of e-cigarette products is not completely harmless. 5 For example, e-cigarettes have been shown to have a negative impact on both the cardiovascular and respiratory systems. 6 A recent study by Mohammadi et al 7 found that chronic e-cigarette users have diminished blood vessel function, particularly impaired release of endothelial nitric oxide and decreased flow-mediated dilation. Also, a systematic review published in 2023 found that the risk of myocardial infarction was lower in e-cigarette users compared with traditional tobacco smokers, but higher than in never-smokers. 8 The term E-cigarette or Vaping product use-Associated Lung Injury (EVALI) was created in 2019, 9 whereby e-cigarette users can experience severe lung damage and hypoxaemia, often requiring respiratory support. The aetiology of EVALI is currently unknown, but vitamin E acetate, a component of many e-cigarette products, has been suggested as a potential contributor. 9 E-cigarette use may also worsen existing asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). 10 Furthermore, a recent systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrated that dual use of tobacco and e-cigarettes significantly increases the risk of both cardiovascular and respiratory outcomes compared with cigarette-only users, suggesting increased harm from the addition of e-cigarette use. 11

E-cigarettes may also have an impact on one’s participation and performance in physical activity, further contributing to its potential for negative health consequences. 12 This association is likely multifactorial and influenced by a combination of behavioural and physiologic factors. For example, those who use e-cigarettes may partake in increased sedentary behaviours, such as social media use or screen time. 13 14 Increased sedentary time has been correlated with poorer cardiorespiratory fitness, independent of physical activity levels, in multiple studies. 15 16 Current data on the relationship between physical activity participation and e-cigarettes appear to be mixed, with some studies reporting increased physical activity in e-cigarette users and others reporting a decrease in activity participation. 12 17 18 Additionally, chronic changes in cardiovascular and respiratory function induced by e-cigarettes may also negatively impact fitness performance. 19 20 Optimal cardiovascular and respiratory function is crucial for effective oxygen delivery to tissues and removal of CO2, which are important to maintain aerobic capacity. 21 Cardiorespiratory fitness is an important contributor to positive health and longevity. Maximal oxygen uptake (VO2 max), the gold standard for assessing cardiorespiratory fitness, has been inversely associated with all-cause mortality in multiple studies. 22 23

Understanding the impact of e-cigarettes on physical activity and cardiorespiratory fitness will contribute to a better understanding of the potential health outcomes associated with e-cigarette use. This has important implications for both conventional cigarette smokers looking to switch to e-cigarettes, and for youth and young adults who may currently, or in future, vape recreationally. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic review synthesising the evidence on the association of e-cigarettes with exercise participation and aerobic capacity. Thus, we aim to conduct a systematic review looking at markers of cardiorespiratory fitness and physical activity in e-cigarette users compared with non-users. The following protocol describes our planned methodology and analysis plan.
sections.methods:
The methods of this systematic review protocol are reported in alignment with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols guidelines. 24 This review has also been registered on PROSPERO (CRD420250589685).

Our research question in the context of the population, intervention, comparison, outcomes, study time (PICOT) framework is described below.

All studies with human participants will be considered eligible for inclusion. There will be no restrictions applied based on gender, age, ethnicity or the presence of health comorbidities. This decision was made to promote greater generalisability of our findings across a broader population.

We will consider users of all types of Electronic Nicotine Delivery Systems to be eligible, including users of e-cigarettes, and both nicotine and non-nicotine vaping device users. To qualify as regular users, participants should report evidence of recent use, such as at least one instance of e-cigarette use reported within the past 30 days. Studies that involve concurrent use of multiple products (eg, e-cigarettes and traditional cigarettes) will also be eligible for inclusion. Though the inclusion of this group may lead to additional challenges in isolating the direct effects of e-cigarettes, it still provides valuable information about e-cigarette use. For instance, comparisons can be made between dual users and those who exclusively smoke cigarettes.

Our intent is to compare current e-cigarette users—defined as individuals who report any e-cigarette use within the past 30 days, including daily, weekly or occasional (less than monthly) use—against non-users of e-cigarette products. Non-users will be more precisely categorised as follows: (1) never-users, referring to individuals who have never used e-cigarettes and never smoked cigarettes; (2) exclusive cigarette smokers, defined as individuals who currently smoke cigarettes (ie, any smoking in the past 30 days) but do not use e-cigarettes and (3) former smokers, defined as individuals who have quit smoking cigarettes and have never used e-cigarettes. We will avoid grouping former e-cigarette users under ‘non-users’ to ensure clarity between never-users and ex-users.

The outcomes we will consider include markers of cardiorespiratory fitness or physical activity participation. For cardiorespiratory fitness, this may include but is not limited to VO2 max, timed run and walk tests, and peak metabolic equivalents of task (METs). For physical activity participation, this may include but is not limited to weekly hours of sport or physical activity participation and frequency of meeting the Canadian Physical Activity Guidelines.

Eligible studies published after database inception will be included. There will be no restriction based on study duration or length of follow-up.

To better align with real-world patterns of use, we will exclude studies that only examine the effects of a single vaping session, as these may not capture the total physiologic impact on exercise capacity in regular users. Additionally, studies which exclusively report on standard markers of cardiovascular or respiratory function (eg, heart rate, forced expiratory volume in 1 s, etc) will be excluded, as these effects have already been summarised in previously published systematic reviews. 25 27

The proposed timeline for this study is from September 2024 to September 2025. A literature search was conducted in October 2024 across PubMed/MEDLINE, Cochrane Library and Embase to identify relevant studies. Eligible studies published after database inception will be included, with no restriction to date or language of publication. The search terms used to aid the search strategy were developed based on the PICOT eligibility criteria and included (“Vaping” OR “Vapi*” OR “E-cigarette*” OR “E-Cig*” OR “electronic cigarette*” OR “ENDS, electronic nicotine delivery system”) AND (“VO2” OR “VO2max” OR “maximum VO2” OR “Aerobic capacity” OR “Aerobic performance” OR “Exercise capacity” OR “Cardiorespiratory fitness” OR “Fitness” OR “Exercise” OR “6MWT” OR “6 minute walk test” OR “Treadmill test” OR “2-mile run” OR “12-minute run” OR “Maximal oxygen uptake” OR “maximum oxygen uptake” OR “oxygen consumption” OR “Physical activity”). The complete search strategy and syntax are presented in online supplemental file 1 .

Study designs that will be accepted include, but are not limited to, randomised controlled trials (RCTs), case–control studies, cohort studies, cross-sectional studies and quasi-experimental studies. Conference presentations, editorials, letters, case studies, systematic reviews, grey literature and retracted articles will be excluded. We anticipate there may be relevant studies which have received industry funding or other conflicts of interest, which may lead to increased likelihood of publication if they report favourable findings of e-cigarette device use. Recognising this limitation, we will not exclude those studies declaring a conflict of interest, but we will make note of these studies and the reported conflict.

The results of the search will be uploaded to Covidence, an online platform which facilitates collaboration among team members and completion of the systematic review process. Title and abstracts will be independently screened by two reviewers according to the PICOT and eligibility criteria. The full texts of the included studies will then be independently assessed by two reviewers. The reason for exclusion of studies at the full text stage will be recorded. Any discrepancies throughout the process will be resolved by consultation with a third reviewer.

We also plan to apply a forward citation search strategy as an adjunct to our primary search strategy to capture additional relevant articles. This decision was made in an effort to improve the comprehensiveness of our literature search and identify studies which may not be retrieved with the keywords or search terms but are similar in context or methodology to the included studies. 28 29 For all articles accepted after full text review in the primary search, we will use citation indexing tools (eg, Google Scholar) to systematically review and evaluate newer publications that cited these articles. Title and abstracts will be screened according to the same criteria as outlined above for the primary search. Articles deemed to be relevant will then undergo full text review by two reviewers.

For the studies that are ultimately accepted for inclusion in the review, the following data will be extracted from each included study: study design and methodology (eg, cross-sectional, prospective, retrospective); number of participants in each group; participant demographics and baseline characteristics (eg, mean age, gender, relevant comorbidities); duration of e-cigarette use; comparator group (eg, cigarette smoker, never smoker); specific outcome measured and results of each group (including mean±SD); follow-up duration and loss to follow-up. Two reviewers will be responsible for the initial extraction of data. A third reviewer will be consulted to resolve disagreements.

We anticipate that case–control and cohort studies will represent the majority of included study designs. Thus, the Newcastle-Ottawa scale will be used to assess the risk of bias of these studies. 30 If any RCTs are included, they will be assessed using the Cochrane Risk-of-bias tool (version 2). 31 Subsequently, the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation framework will be used to assess the certainty and strength of evidence. 32

Data will be synthesised by grouping studies according to similar exposure categories (eg, exclusive e-cigarette users, dual users, non-users, former users) and outcome measures (eg, cardiorespiratory fitness marker vs physical activity participation marker). This approach will allow for structured comparison across similar exposure-outcome profiles. Primary comparisons will be conducted between exclusive e-cigarette users and non-users to better isolate the effects of e-cigarettes. Dual users will be analysed separately, recognising that their combined exposure makes it difficult to attribute effects solely due to e-cigarette use.

Our primary outcome of interest will be the mean difference in cardiorespiratory fitness markers (eg, VO2 max, walk/run tests) in e-cigarette users compared with non-users. Our secondary outcome will be the mean difference in physical activity levels (eg, weekly hours of sport participation, frequency of meeting physical activity guidelines) in e-cigarette users compared with non-users. While these outcomes are related and often correlate with each other, they offer unique information. Cardiorespiratory fitness is strongly linked to cardiovascular and metabolic health, while physical activity can be influenced by an individual’s lifestyle and behaviours. 33 Analysing both these metrics will offer a more comprehensive picture of the overall health and fitness of e-cigarette users and offer some preliminary insight as to whether differences in physical activity patterns may influence the cardiorespiratory fitness of e-cigarette users.

Study heterogeneity will be assessed using the I² statistic. We will consider a meta-analysis feasible if at least three studies are available for a given comparison and outcome, and if heterogeneity is moderate (I² <60%) or can be explained through subgroup analyses. Efforts will be made to pool data and conduct a meta-analysis if sufficient data and homogeneity are present. Otherwise, a narrative synthesis will be conducted, focusing on common themes, subgroups and sources of variability. Separate meta-analyses will be conducted for different study designs (eg, cross-sectional vs cohort studies) and for specific comparisons, such as e-cigarette users vs never-tobacco smokers, e-cigarette users versus current smokers and e-cigarette users versus former smokers, where data permit. For example, we will attempt to stratify studies according to the age of participants, type of product use (exclusive e-cigarette users vs dual e-cigarette and combustive cigarette users), funding source (tobacco industry funded vs non-funded by industries) and their comorbidities, where data are available. Analyses will also consider stratification by presence or absence of specific comorbidities (eg, asthma, COPD, cardiovascular disease) to explore potential effect modification. Different age groups (eg, adolescents, young adults, older adults) may have differences in baseline cardiorespiratory fitness, patterns of e-cigarette use and physiological vulnerability, which may influence the observed results. Furthermore, underlying health conditions such as COPD or cardiovascular disease may modify the relationship between e-cigarettes and fitness through impaired respiratory or cardiovascular reserve. 9

Patients and members of the public have not been involved in the design or conduct of this review but will be engaged to support reporting and dissemination of study results.
sections.discussion:
This will be the first systematic review to comprehensively summarise the literature regarding the effects of e-cigarette use on markers of cardiorespiratory fitness and participation in physical activity.

This research will contribute to the growing body of evidence related to the health consequences of regular e-cigarette use. We anticipate that e-cigarettes will have a detrimental impact on exercise participation and cardiorespiratory fitness, given the preliminary research available to date. 12 34 However, the magnitude of this effect may be influenced by the comparator group (ie, cigarette smokers vs non-smokers), the duration of e-cigarette use and the specific protocol used for measuring cardiorespiratory fitness.

We recognise there are a few limitations and barriers relevant to this review. First, there may be a limited number of research studies which evaluate the long-term health effects of e-cigarettes. 9 One explanation for this lack of research is that these devices only recently entered the consumer markets, beginning at the onset of the 21st century. 9 Several decades’ worth of follow-up will likely be necessary to establish conclusive causative evidence. Moreover, there may be an element of publication bias from studies that are funded by device companies, such that studies which report unfavourable results in e-cigarette users may be less likely to be published. Second, the sample sizes of studies may be small, thus limiting their statistical power. Heterogeneity of studies, as discussed above, may also be a barrier which will make analysis and interpretation of the data more challenging. Fourth, we anticipate many of the included studies will use a cross-sectional design. As such, inferences about the directionality or causality of any observed associations will be limited. Taken together, these factors may make it more difficult to draw firm conclusions and findings will need to be interpreted with appropriate caution.

Nonetheless, summarising the existing data on this topic offers several important benefits. First, it will offer preliminary evidence as to the impact of e-cigarettes on physical performance and exercise capabilities. These results will be of importance for people who use e-cigarettes or may consider vaping, either to quit smoking or recreationally. They will also be of interest to healthcare providers, administrators and policy-makers, especially given the rise in e-cigarette use. 1 Additionally, it may identify specific areas in which data are lacking, providing avenues for future research to be conducted.

Ethics approval is not required for this specific review. The results of the review will be disseminated via conference presentations and peer-reviewed publication. Moreover, results of this review may inform public health recommendations and identify areas in the field where further research is needed.
